title: Even Owning a Cell Phone Is Bad for Kids’ Test Scores
gist: A UCLA study in Behavioral Sciences on 106 third- and sixth-graders found that having a phone physically present made no measurable difference to reading comprehension scores, undercutting the premise of the bell-to-bell school phone bans Illinois just enacted. Note the discrepancy with the headline: the body text as captured reports only the null result on phone presence and never substantiates the claim that mere ownership depresses scores.

insights.claim: UCLA psychologists tested 55 sixth-graders and 51 third-graders, having phone-owning children take two reading comprehension tests — one with the phone present and one with it removed — and found essentially no difference in scores between the two conditions.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: A within-subject null on the mechanism everyone assumes is real; small n (106) means this is a caution flag rather than a refutation, but it is the kind of result that stalls policy momentum.
insights.quote: Those who had their phones out performed about the same as those with no phones.

insights.claim: Researchers offer 'nomophobia' — anxiety from separation from one's phone, a portmanteau of 'no mobile phobia' — as one explanation for the null result, on the theory that phone absence may be as distracting as phone presence.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: If separation anxiety substitutes one-for-one for notification distraction, confiscation-based policies buy nothing — the relevant intervention target is attachment, not access.
insights.quote: the anxiety that comes from being separated from a cell phone (and yes, it’s a portmanteau of “no mobile phobia”)

insights.claim: The researchers noted an alternative and more mundane explanation for the null: children with phones simply did not receive enough notifications during the test window for interruption effects to register.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: A short test window with low notification volume is a design limitation, not evidence of no effect — the finding may not generalize to a full school day.
insights.quote: the kids with phones didn’t receive enough notifications during the tests to make much of a difference

insights.claim: Illinois Governor JB Pritzker signed a bill directing state school districts to implement a bell-to-bell cell phone ban starting next school year, a mandate the new research suggests may not raise test scores.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: State-level bell-to-bell mandates are spreading faster than the evidence base supporting them; a growing null literature is the tail risk to the phone-pouch and device-management vendors selling into those mandates.
insights.quote: New research hints that school cell phone bans may not be enough
